articles.title: Kenyan doomsday sect leader jailed for 200 years for murder of 190 children
articles.summary: Paul Mackenzie convicted over deaths of children and one adult after followers were ordered to starve themselves and their families
body: The leader of a Kenyan doomsday sect has been sentenced to 200 years in prison for the murders of 190 children and one adult in one of the world’s worst cult disasters in recent history.

The sentence, comprising 100 years for murder by starvation and 100 years by direct homicide, came two weeks after the court in Kenya’s coastal city of Mombasa found the cult leader guilty of the crimes.

Prosecutors said Paul Mackenzie and his Good News International church ran ​a Christian doomsday sect whose members were ordered to starve themselves and their children to death to go to heaven before the world ended.
His accomplices threatened and beat victims to ensure they followed his orders. The emaciated bodies were found scattered in shallow graves and dumped in latrines. Some had been buried alive.
Mackenzie was arrested in 2023 after police received a tipoff, and weeks later authorities began uncovering bodies in shallow graves in the Shakahola forest near the coast in south-eastern Kenya.
In total, more than 400 bodies have been recovered. Many were severely decomposed and only 26 could be identified.
Mackenzie denied murder charges, saying he did not force the victims to starve, but the court rejected that argument.
The Shakahola tragedy has gripped Kenya since the discovery of mass graves in the forest more than three years ago.
It raised questions about how Mackenzie was able to continue operating despite being on the radar of the authorities since 2017, when police searched his premises.
In 2019, authorities shut down Mackenzie’s church and he relocated ‌to the Shakahola forest, police said.
The case has also led to calls for tougher oversight of churches and other religious organisations in a country where religious faith plays a prominent role in public life.
Mackenzie, a former taxi driver, forbade cult members from sending their children to school and from going to hospital when they were ill, describing such institutions as satanic.
Cult members lived in makeshift homes of polythene sheeting and thatch that Mackenzie divided into areas with biblical names such as Jerusalem and Judea.
The plight of his followers began ​to emerge in March 2023, when a man told ​police his brother and wife had starved their children ​to death in the forest on Mackenzie’s orders.

Mackenzie was arrested but released on bail, after which relatives said he brought forward the date ​on which he told his followers the ‌world would end. Police rearrested him and ​started combing through the forest more systematically and began exhuming mass graves.
Last month’s judgment covered 191 deaths while investigations into more than 200 other deaths are continuing.
Justice Diana Kavedza-Mochache said in a hearing lasting more than eight hours that in some cases children were isolated and denied food while their parents watched.
Mackenzie faces other charges over the forest deaths, including those of terrorism, which he has denied.
Prosecutors said that while he was in detention he also directed the deaths of 52 people in Kwa Binzaro village, about 18 miles from Shakahola. Mackenzie has pleaded not guilty in that case.

articles.title: Flávio Bolsonaro battles to remain relevant as he speaks at rightwing conference at Mar-a-Lago
articles.summary: Far-right politician addresses Conservative Political Action Conference and makes unsubstantiated claims about election fraud
body: Flávio Bolsonaro, the far-right politician who lost Brazil’s presidential election last month, has insisted his defeat is not “the end for Brazil” as he battles to maintain political relevance after fleeing to the US.
Bolsonaro absconded early last week shortly after losing the 25 October election to the leftwing incumbent Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva by more than 4m votes.

On Thursday night Bolsonaro made his first major public appearance since arriving in the US, speaking at a rightwing gathering at Donald Trump’s Mar-a-Lago property where he claimed “great things” were still to come.

“I know this wasn’t the end for Brazil and I know it wasn’t the end for America,” Bolsonaro, 45, told a gala dinner at the Conservative Political Action Conference (CPAC)’s four-day “gathering of visionaries” event, where the former British prime minister Liz Truss is also due to speak.

“Even when what seems like the end isn’t what we’d hoped for, we must thank God and have even more faith that this isn’t yet the end,” he added. “No one shuts the door that he opens – and the door he shuts, no one opens.”
Earlier, in his first post-election interview, Bolsonaro made a series of unsubstantiated claims about election fraud and insisted he received “help from absolutely no one” to flee.

“It was all me,” Bolsonaro told the New York Times, contradicting reports that he was helped by the Trump adviser Jason Miller and Santiago Caputo, a close aide to Argentina’s rightwing president, Javier Milei.

He said he would “take to the grave” the full story of how he had fled Brazil, where he faces federal police investigations for money laundering and corruption. Bolsonaro is a member of congress who has held elected office for more than 20 years but he will lose parliamentary immunity early next year when his term ends, meaning he could then be prosecuted.

Brazilian analysts agree that by skipping the country after an election in which he received 59m votes, Bolsonaro, the son of jailed former president Jair Bolsonaro, abdicated leadership of the opposition and sabotaged his political future.

Thomas Traumann, an author and pundit for the TV network GloboNews, said: “Flávio was foolish enough to throw away the leadership of the opposition that he could have exercised had he stayed in Brazil. But the [Bolsonaro] family is still a player.”

Flávio Bolsonaro’s brother, the former congressman Eduardo Bolsonaro, also lives in self-imposed exile in the US and will have to serve a four-year sentence for coercion if he returns to Brazil. Four other members of the Bolsonaro family were elected to congress in last month’s election, including their brothers Carlos and Jair Renan and stepmother, Michelle Bolsonaro.

Traumann believed it was not inconceivable that Jair Bolsonaro would attempt a political comeback if he managed to negotiate his way out of his 27-year prison sentence for plotting a coup after losing the 2022 election to Lula. However, as things stand, the 71-year-old is banned from running for office until 2060 and must live under house arrest.
Many doubt the Bolsonaro family can continue to control Bolsonarismo, the populist political movement that takes their name, with two key members in exile and one imprisoned.
“[The movement] is mortally wounded because of its mistakes and its crimes,” the political scientist Sérgio Abranches told the newspaper O Globo this week.

Abranches said democratic rightwing politicians now had a chance to “detach” themselves from the Bolsonaros’ anti-democratic movement and break off in a new direction before the next presidential election in 2030.
Flávio Bolsonaro told the New York Times he would “obviously” be a candidate in future elections but said his future lay in the US “at least for now”.

It is unclear where Flávio Bolsonaro, who has been granted a US visa by Trump, will live. His brother Eduardo set up home in Southlake, Texas, after leaving Brazil last year – although some expect him to move after the traditionally conservative state elected the Democrat Gina Hinojosa as governor in this week’s midterms.

In a video posted on CPAC’s social networks before Thursday’s event, Eduardo Bolsonaro played down the risk posed by the “blue tsunami” to their ability to stay in the US. “They [Democrats] will try [to make trouble for us] – but it’s not up to Congress … to revoke visas or citizenships,” he said.
Likening their plight to that of a female asylum seeker fleeing Iran for fear of being killed after refusing to wear a hijab, he added: “I am 100% legal – as is my brother and his family.”

articles.title: ANC faces bruising defeat in South African local elections with 80% of ballots counted
articles.summary: Former liberation movement’s share of national vote almost 14 percentage points below 2021 result
body: The African National Congress is on course to suffer a bruising defeat in South Africa’s local elections, with the once dominant party of Nelson Mandela falling to under a third of the vote nationally with more than 80% of ballots counted.

Wednesday’s fragmented vote marks another stage in the decline of the ANC, which has led national governments since the end of white minority apartheid rule in 1994. High unemployment, crime, corruption and poor local service delivery have all contributed to voters turning away from the party.

The former liberation movement is projected to lose its status as the biggest party in the two most populous provinces, Gauteng and KwaZulu-Natal, as parties began coalition negotiations behind closed doors. The final results are expected to be announced on Sunday.

The ANC was on 31.8% of the vote nationally, almost 14 percentage points below its 2021 local election result. The centre-right, white-led Democratic Alliance (DA) had 24.1% of the vote, while the uMkhonto weSizwe (MK) party of the former ANC president Jacob Zuma was on 9.3%.
Turnout also rose in Wednesday’s poll. The election commission estimated that 54.5% of registered voters cast their ballot, up from 46% five years ago.

The final shape of coalitions in some of the country’s biggest cities remained unclear with the final votes still being counted. Senior figures in key parties said they would talk with almost anyone, while keeping negotiating strategies under wraps.

In Johannesburg, South Africa’s commercial capital and biggest city, with 4.8 million people, voters have had to contend with regular water and power cuts, uncollected rubbish and potholes. The municipality, which has seen 10 changes of mayor in the last decade amid unstable coalitions, has admitted to a 220bn rand (£9.9bn) infrastructure spending backlog.

With just over half of votes counted in Johannesburg, the DA was leading with 40%, having run an energetic campaign under Helen Zille, a 75-year-old former Cape Town mayor. The ANC, which leads the current coalition, was in second place on 17.5%. ActionSA, a rightwing party led by Herman Mashaba, was on 15.5%. Mashaba has pledged never to work with Zille, whom he calls “racist”, something she vehemently denies.

Many of the ANC’s township strongholds have yet to report full results. The Council for Scientific and Industrial Research (CSIR), a respected thinktank, has projected the DA will finish with 34%, the ANC 20% and ActionSA 16.8%.
Coalitions in Gauteng’s three city municipalities are often negotiated together. The DA is leading in all three.

The MK party, led by 84-year-old Zuma as he continues to weather and deny numerous corruption allegations, is expected to displace the ANC as the largest party in KwaZulu-Natal. Founded in 2023, it mixes socially conservative Zulu nationalism with pledges to redistribute land and wealth from white to black South Africans.

With half of votes counted in eThekwini municipality, which contains Durban, the MK had 41%, meaning other parties could form a coalition to keep it out of power. Meanwhile, the DA is projected to maintain its majority in Cape Town, despite growing middle-class anger over rising housing costs.
Voters choose a local councillor and a party, with seats allocated via proportional representation. Councillors will then have two weeks to elect mayors and form municipal governments.

articles.title: ‘We’ve been preparing for the worst all year’: uncertainty grips Iran after Trump midterms defeat
articles.summary: While some fear another full-scale war, others are less sure – but both agree repression at home will continue
body: Just hours after the US midterm election results delivered a crushing defeat for the Republican party, pro-regime crowds gathered in Tehran’s Enghelab Square to set fire to a giant banner depicting Donald Trump, his vice-president, JD Vance, the US envoy Steve Witkoff and the Israeli prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu.
Iranian officials have since issued defiant statements celebrating the Republican losses, portraying the results as a rejection of Trump’s war against Iran.
Iran’s supreme leader, Mojtaba Khamenei, whose father and predecessor, Ali Khamenei, was killed during strikes in February, said: “The process of the US’s collapse has accelerated.”

In another display, Iranian state television broadcast footage of a mock hanging of Trump in Tehran’s Tajrish Square that featured an actor wearing a mask of the US president and an orange prison uniform.

Inside the country, however, some Iranians describe a sense of apprehension, pointing to the worsening economic situation and uncertainty over what Trump’s political setback could mean for their future.
For Mehnaz, a Tehran-based journalist, the mood is one of hopelessness, as people struggle to make sense of what lies ahead.

“I am really fearful. Of what? I still don’t know. It’s a weird feeling,” she said. “Frankly, it’s a truly strange scenario here. People have set their sights on the US and Israel, hoping that this will bring change. I found that very strange and still do.”
Some of those she has spoken to believe that Trump’s midterm loss could make another full-scale war more likely.

“Many think since this is Trump’s second term, and he therefore doesn’t need to be re-elected, he might continue the war,” she said. “But what worries me is that the [Iranian] regime has been executing people daily and this is only getting worse, with or without war.”
According to the Oslo-based NGO Iran Human Rights (IHR), Iranian authorities have executed at least 696 people this year.
Alborz, a 36-year-old writer in Tehran, said the appearance of ordinary life masked an increasingly precarious reality.

“In the shops, people can still be seen browsing for clothes and other goods, just as before. Yet actual purchases have become rare, and a single T-shirt now costs what a full suit might have set you back a year ago,” he said.

“Amid the banter and everyday chatter, you overhear passersby debating whether a kerosene heater is better than a wood-burning one, readying themselves, in their own way, for the possibility that the infrastructure may one day be destroyed.
“It is a resilience born of compulsion. There is nothing noble in it,” added Alborz.

Unlike those who fear Trump’s defeat could bring renewed conflict, Alborz said people around him appeared to believe the likelihood of another full-scale war had diminished. “There’s a general feeling that with what happened in the US election and with Israel, the likelihood of a full-scale war resuming has decreased. Still, no one is certain.”

But while Iranians who are opposed to the government differ over whether another war is likely, a common fear among those interviewed is that the repression at home will continue regardless of what happens in the US.

For Noor, 24, a resident of Karaj who spent three weeks in prison after taking part in protests in January, that fear has only intensified. “They arrested me during the war, so their repression mechanism is like a well-oiled machine which won’t stop working whether it’s under clouds or bombs.”

Asked how she felt about the days ahead following Trump’s midterm defeat, she said uncertainty had become a part of life. “If someone tells you inside the country what they predict will happen next, they are lying. No one, absolutely no one, knows what will happen. We have been preparing for the worst all year.
“But I know what won’t happen. This repression will not end,” said Noor.

Moein, a medic in central Iran, believed the US and the west underestimated the strength of Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), particularly the loyalty of its personnel and its strategic capabilities.

“Even I underestimated how powerful and strategically well placed the IRGC is,” he said. “I used to think, or at least like to think of the whole system as fossilised mullahs and corrupt, out-of-touch military men. But it’s clear to me now that they’re somewhat competent. And still loyal, despite how corrupt they can be.”

For Moein, that recognition has brought a bitter sense of contradiction: “A state capable of enduring decades of sanctions and confronting the world’s most powerful military, yet willing to turn its coercive machinery against its own population.”
“It’s a shame, really. For them to fight back against the sole superpower of the world and last half a century under sanctions, only to kill young girls in the streets.”
Asked whether he expected world leaders to react to the continuing repression in Iran, he said he had fewer and fewer expectations of the European leaders.
For Mehnaz, the celebrations by pro-government crowds were only getting more “outrageous” by the day. “And why won’t they celebrate? They [IRGC] have just found a hope for survival,” she said.

articles.title: Russia and US seek to block plan for binding rules on autonomous weapons
articles.summary: UN conference this month seen as key moment after years of discussions on filling gap in governance of AI systems
body: Plans to fill a gap in the global governance of autonomous weapons are in jeopardy as a group of nations led by Russia and the US move to use a UN conference this month to block proposals to negotiate a legally binding set of rules.

The scale of the opposition will become clear at a diplomatic retreat starting on Friday before the seventh review conference on “certain conventional weapons” in Geneva due to be attended by 128 countries from 16 to 20 November.

The review conference is seen as the key moment when the world could decide whether to back a mandate to negotiate a legally binding instrument negotiated within a defined timetable. The speed with which autonomous weapons are being developed and used in warfare is widely acknowledged.

Anna Hehir, the head of military AI governance at the Future of Life Institute, an independent nonprofit, said: “States have never been closer to launching a global agreement on AI weapons. A lot of the hard work has already been done and states have now agreed by consensus to elements of a draft treaty text that would be the basis for negotiations to start.

“But we will likely see some states hide behind language that has the veneer of progress but advocates for a continuation of endless discussions on voluntary measures that have no teeth. The proposals for more years of discussions on non-legally binding measures are smokescreens to keep autonomous weapons systems unregulated and states unaccountable for their use.”

Discussions have been under way on the issue inside the UN for nearly three years but Russia, the US and Israel, among others, are pushing against the review conference setting a timetable for a legally binding instrument.

In an intervention timed to influence the review conference, Pope Leo XIV stressed that decisions relating to human life could never be given to machines. He said: “Decisions affecting human life, freedom and the use of force must always remain subject to effective, informed and responsible human oversight. For this reason, artificial intelligence must be ‘disarmed’, and I encourage the states meeting in Geneva in November to take concrete steps toward banning lethal autonomous weapons.”

Human Rights Watch and the campaign group Stop Killer Robots argue that weapons systems, assisted by AI, are proven to behave unpredictably, increasing the risk of fatal errors and battlefields spinning out of human control.

The International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC) said on Thursday: “The time has come to move from discussion to negotiation on new international rules to regulate autonomous systems. The world cannot afford further delays.”

In July, Ukraine reported for the first time that Russia had used an AI-guided drone, which struck a propane tank at a fuel station in Zaporizhzhia. The Ukrainian president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, has warned about the speed of AI weapon development, calling for the Ukraine war to be ended before AI takes over the battlefield.

On 22 October, a coalition of 50 states including Ireland, Italy, Brazil, Mexico, France and Germany called for the conference to agree a strict negotiating mandate. The ICRC separately reported that more than 70 states supported beginning negotiations on a legal instrument.
The UK did not back the Irish statement and has previously argued that existing international humanitarian law is sufficient basis for the regulation of such weapons.

The Ireland-led group proposed a mandate to be agreed by the review conference that would establish a time-limited expert group tasked with negotiating the needed rules over three sessions in Geneva in 2027, totalling 25 days. The group would be required to submit a report containing the draft protocol to that year’s annual meeting, expected to take place later in 2027.

In September, a UN experts group report prepared for the Geneva review conference tried to define the moral issues at stake by backing general calls for human judgment and control in the use of such weapons, as well as limits on the range and breadth with which they are allowed to operate.

The French government welcomed the experts group proposals, saying they were a sufficient basis for the conference to be given a negotiating mandate that “bans completely autonomous weapons systems and regulates systems with autonomous functions”.

The US largely favours leaving it to nation states to impose their controls in line with international humanitarian law. The Pentagon has set up its own autonomous weapons working group. Similar expert committees in Germany are trying to define the principles behind how human control can be exerted over such weapons.
Related: It’s not hypothetical: the dangers of AI are already here | Granate Kim and Mohamed Hussein

In August the outgoing UN secretary general, António Guterres, and the ICRC president, Mirjana Spoljaric, warned that the world was “nearing a moral red line where autonomous weapons could kill without human involvement”. They said: “Negotiations must begin now to urgently adopt a legally binding instrument to regulate autonomous weapon systems with clear prohibitions and restrictions.”

A recent poll commissioned by the Future of Life Institute found overwhelming support for a global treaty to limit AI weapons among the public in France, Germany and the UK, but some scepticism that the treaty would ever be respected.

A total of 163 states voted at the UN disarmament and international security committee that they were ready to launch negotiations. They will face enormous pressure to back down and settle for outcomes that keep the issue deadlocked. Multilateral arms control agreements are known to come about when cross-regional majorities withstand pressure and step outside of consensus paralysis.
The expert working group defined autonomous weapons as those weapons “capable of identifying, selecting and engaging a target without the need to refer the issue to a human being”.

The latest example of the misuse of AI in war was the US bombing of a school in Minab, Iran, on 28 February, which killed at least 175 people. The targeting included input from the Maven AI system operated by Palantir. Maven reportedly did not flag that the site was now a school, nor did any personnel tasked with reviewing the AI target data. One advantage of AI is that it is much quicker in checking a target list, but no one picked up that this target had been a school for 10 years.

articles.title: Denmark’s top court to rule on ‘parallel societies’ after ‘non-western’ people evicted
articles.summary: Government claims removal of former residents of housing complex in Helsingør is unrelated to their ethnicity
body: Denmark’s supreme court is expected to rule on whether the state’s classification of residents with “non-western” backgrounds is covered by racial discrimination law.

The appeal by residents who were evicted from Nøjsomhed-Sydvej in Helsingør, a city north of Copenhagen, could have far-reaching implications for others who have been forced out of their homes by the controversial legislation previously known as the “ghetto law”. The government now refers to affected neighbourhoods as “parallel societies”.

The residents, who have been unsuccessful in other courts, argue that the evictions by the housing association were intended to cut the number of residents with a “non-western” background in order to stop the area from becoming a “ghetto” and therefore subject to the legislation. The government has previously argued the classification is unrelated to ethnicity.

In December, the European court of justice (ECJ) ruled that the legislation may be unlawful. The law requires housing associations to cut not-for-profit housing by 40%, including by selling or demolishing properties or terminating the lease of tenants by 2030.
Related: Copenhagen’s ‘ghetto law’ may be unlawful, EU court rules

It also includes demolishing apartment blocks in areas previously labelled “tough ghettos” (now “transformation areas”) by the government, where at least half of residents have a “non-western” background. Other areas with similar socioeconomic conditions – such as high levels of unemployment or crime – are not subject to these measures.

The policy has been widely criticised by human rights groups including Amnesty International. The European Commission Against Racism and Intolerance published a report last month that said there had been “no positive change in the authorities’ approach to the use of the ‘non-western’ category across various laws, policies and administrative practices, including in relation to the ‘parallel society’ legislation”.

The UN committee on the elimination of racial discrimination has called on Danish authorities to stop using the terms “western” and “non-western” in law and policy, and expressed concern that the parallel societies law has a “discriminatory impact on ethnic minorities”.

Residents in Mjølnerparken housing estate in central Copenhagen, who filed a suit against the law in Denmark in 2020 arguing that using their ethnicity to decide where they can live was discriminatory and illegal, have yet to have their case returned to the domestic courts since December’s verdict. More than 1,000 people were forced to move out because of the law.

But legal experts said that the Nøjsomhed-Sydvej case, to be heard on Friday and Monday, could have implications for the Mjølnerparken case because it is likely to lead to a domestic ruling on whether “non-western” background is covered by racial discrimination law.

Susheela Math, the head of legal at the NGO Systemic Justice, said: “If the supreme court decides that ‘non-western’ background is linked to ethnic origin and racial discrimination law, that raises huge questions for the Danish state.”
Related: Top EU court adviser finds Denmark’s ‘ghetto law’ is direct discrimination
It would force the Danish state to decide whether it is to abolish the categorisation entirely, which could have ramifications across society, she said.

“[The government] will refer to ethnic origin when it suits them but inside a court, no matter what you present, they say ‘non-western’ background has nothing to do with ethnicity and that they do not collect ethnic data,” said Math.
It is understood that residents of Nøjsomhed-Sydvej would be allowed to return to their homes if they win the case, expected to be decided later this month.
But it is likely to be much more difficult for residents of Mjølnerparken to return to their homes if they win their case when it is heard, because they have been sold.
The Danish ministry of children, senior citizens, and housing has been contacted for comment.

articles.title: Friday briefing: ​After a week of disruption, is living with threats our new normal?
articles.summary: In today’s newsletter: From diverted airliners to hacked ​fridges, a string of disruptive incidents has exposed the ​vulnerabilities of modern ​life. ​There is now an increasingly blurred space between peace and conflict, the grey zone
body: Good morning. A multiplicity of hoax bomb threats divert passenger flights across Europe. A malign cyber-attack targets supermarket fridges in Belgium, Sweden, the UK and – in a sickening escalation – the cold storage facilities of France’s national blood service.

The actors behind this week of chaos and disruption, be they hostile states or criminal gangs – or even enterprising teenagers – are yet to be identified. But what is certain is that they operate in a context of deepening global conflicts, building national threat and an accompanying, pervasive sense of vulnerability.
Welcome to the grey zone – that ambiguous space between routine peace and conventional military conflict, where proxies duck state accountability and cyber-tactics are developing at an alarming rate.

For today’s newsletter, I spoke to the Guardian’s defence and security editor, Dan Sabbagh, and our global technology team about flights, fridges and why “keep calm and carry on” is more than a tote bag slogan.
UK news | Russell Brand has been found guilty of raping a woman and sexually assaulting three others over the course of five years of his show business career.

US politics | Donald Trump signed a proclamation that he says will prevent future administrations from changing his design of the Oval Office and Cabinet Room, spaces he declared as national monuments that should be preserved.
UK politics | Andy Burnham has said he wants to “recast” the UK’s deal to cede control of the Chagos Islands after resistance from Washington.
Health | Cancer diagnoses in England have hit record highs, with more than 1,000 people a day diagnosed, NHS figures show.
World news | The UN-recognised government of Yemen has shaken up its political and military leadership in an attempt to regain territory lost to the Houthis in September.

Hoax bomb threats disrupted at least 25 different commercial flights across Europe yesterday, with some forced to make emergency landings, and after similar threats on Tuesday, when seven planes were searched or diverted after malicious alerts.

There is, at least so for, no suggestion of orchestration by a hostile terror group or state actor according to investigators, although investigations continue. It’s perfectly possible that this could be the work of some lone disruptors, says Dan, who reminds me that “airlines receive bomb threats on a daily basis, at a rate that we would find extraordinary if we knew”. Nonetheless, the fact that these airlines are treating these threats as credible suggests a potential level of coordination, aviation experts told the Guardian on Thursday.

These threats take place with aviation security under sharper scrutiny after the flydubai incident, when a pilot fought off his knife-wielding colleague in an apparent attempt to crash a full passenger flight heading for Tel Aviv.

But beyond that “jittery background noise”, is a significant step-change in the manner of threat we face. Twenty-five years on from the inception of the War on Terror, when Islamist terrorism has receded relative to the hostile state threats, “we’re living in a different world with familiar uncertainties, but attributed to different players,” Dan tells me.

Conflicts in Ukraine and the Middle East are reverberating closer to home. Since 2022, we’ve witnessed intensifying acts of sabotage on European states that are believed to trace back to Russia but deliberately fall below the threshold for military response – a so-called hybrid or “shadow war” with the singular purpose of disrupting support for Ukraine. Only two months ago, an alleged attack plot on RAF Fairford was organised by a handler police believe was working on behalf of Iran.

Meanwhile, tech expert Azeem Azhar warned recently that the internet is experiencing it’s own Wuhan moment, as AI enables bad actors to hunt for system flaws and spread them, mirroring the early days of the Covid pandemic.
“Terrorism doesn’t have to be violent to terrorise,” says Dan. “The purpose of terrorism is to scare.”

Ratcheting up disruption, and the accompanying psychological hit, is precisely what we’ve seen elsewhere this week. Supermarket fridges and freezers in seven European countries malfunctioned earlier this week, their thermostats remotely cranked up in some cases to 50C, in what some fear indicates a new front in hacking tactics.

Similar incidents have been reported in the UK, and I spoke to our global technology editor Dan Milmo on his way back from interviewing a fruit and veg wholesaler based near Heathrow, whose fridges went on the blink on Monday. The experience has prompted him to add some tinned goods to his weekend shopping list.

“There are only ever two likely candidates for a hack,” Dan tells me. “Criminal gangs or nation states.” He adds an emerging tertiary category of “troublesome teenagers”, such as the loose collective of English-speaking hackers Scattered Spider, two of whom were jailed in July for their attack on Transport for London.

One cybersecurity researcher told Dan that attacks on dummy Danfoss fridge controls – one of the software systems also targeted by the hackers in mainland Europe – had “all the hallmarks” of operations linked to Russia.
What are security services doing about these threats?

“There is a very real and intense cyberwar going on out there,” Dan Sabbagh tells me, and security agencies in the UK have viewed technological resilience as a key part of their responsibility for a number of years. The Turing Institute, for example, is looking at ways to utilise AI to make critical infrastructure systems more secure.

The police and security services are monitoring for threats all the time – MI5 has about 3,000 active subjects of interest currently – arranged in a hierarchy, with an understandable focus on the more serious ones, including threats to life. But lower level activity that is not obviously threatening, whether that’s online activity or buying paint with the intention of daubing racist graffiti, can be harder to pick up. As with other public services, this is a resourcing question as much as anything else.
Is chaos easier to generate in our interconnected world?

I put this to our global technology reporter Aisha Down, who explains that many hacks happen though edge devices – networked items that are connected to the internet but don’t have processing power and so aren’t the main focus of security upgrades by a company or household.
Famously, in 2016, North Korea came within a few keystrokes of pulling off a billion-dollar heist by hacking the Bank of Bangladesh via an unsecured printer.

Aisha is keen to dial down the panic. The point about cyber-attacks is that every single one is opportunistic: a hacker has to find a vulnerability and then discover a way to exploit it. “Just like a burglary, you might get into the room where all the jewellery is stored,” she says, “but the damage you can do is not a given.”

There is, however, a steady escalation in this type of threat. Aisha gives the example of Finland which, given its proximity to Russia, is watching cyber-tactics very closely. “What people report to their national cybersecurity centre is growing, from 18,000 reports last year for a population of 6 million people, to 21,000 this year.” This can be partly traced back to a developing criminal hacking ecosystem, some with loose links to the Russian state.

While a key element of a cyber-attack is the psychological impact, that can be hard to square with the UK government’s own Be Ready initiative, which advises us to off-set threats of hybrid warfare and hostile state sabotage by stockpiling 72 hours’ worth of emergency supplies – including water, beans and Twiglets (if you’re Andy Burnham). Indeed, governments across Europe are advising citizens to build up non-perishable larders.
It’s perhaps useful to balance the likelihood of a cyber-attack with the potential scope, suggests Aisha, who confesses she’s too busy sourcing furniture for her new flat to think about tinned goods.
One European cybersecurity official told Aisha recently that there’s a vulnerability in every 1,500 lines of code, on average.
“Their view is: it’s going to happen. It’s going to be opportunistic. But, unlike bombing a power station in the dead of winter, you won’t be offline for months.”
With that perspective, keeping a bunch of tenners handy to see you through a few days of disruption makes sense.

As for stockpiling food and water, Dan is still debating with his partner just how necessary those extra tins of peas really are. “If you’re a government wanting to spend £10bn more on defence by the end of the decade, it’s useful to have that message about keeping a few bottles of water at home,” he says.

To be clear: it’s not Dan’s intention to dismiss stockpiling advice as a purely cynical exercise. The developing threats are all too real. But as he puts it: “If the purpose of terrorism is to generate fear, the first thing you should do is not panic and keep calm.”

“Brand faces ‘significant’ prison term for rape and sexual assault”, is the Guardian’s front page today. The Times writes “Brand found guilty of rape”, the Telegraph says “BBC ‘enabled’ rapist Brand”, the Sun has “Rapist”, and the Mirror’s take is “Justice”. On the same story, the Mail splashes “Downfall of the swaggering sex predator fawned over by the Left”, and Metro has “Rapist Brand caged”.
Elsewhere, the i Paper leads on “Godfather of AI warns humanity: it’s all hurtling out of control”, and the FT has “Tech stocks plunge as investors worry blue wave will sink AI spending boom”.
Will the UK finally pay slavery reparations?

Andy Burnham has asked countries affected by Britain’s role in slavery to help shape a formal apology through a ‘structured dialogue’. During the prime minister’s visit to the Commonwealth heads of government meeting in Antigua and Barbuda, Downing Street said affected countries would play an indispensable role in crafting an enduring message. Though the plans for talks were received positively, the British government is still ruling out the idea of paying reparations, which for decades campaigners have been calling for. Lucy Hough speaks to the Guardian’s Caribbean correspondent, Natricia Duncan.
A bit of good news to remind you that the world’s not all bad

On 25 October, as Brazil held its presidential election, 101-year-old Celia de Oliveira Soares left home for the first time in months, to vote for the first time in nearly a decade. She was determined that Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva (known as Lula) – who had lost in the first round – should beat the far-right candidate Flávio Bolsonaro.

Since Brazil’s return to democracy in the 1980s, no first-round loser has ever bounced back. But 3 million extra voters took part in the second round, after skipping the first – and 1.4 million of them were over 70 years old. The victorious Lula, along with many others, is now hailing elderly voters as the election’s heroes.
“It is possible to resist fascism – all you need to do is mobilise society,” the former minister Simone Tebet said. “Young people hit the streets and golden-agers saved our democracy.”
